en: The Sūtra on the Fundamental Dharmas of the Primary Noble Portion of Dependent Origination, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying in the city of Śrāvastī at the Jetavana Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.
At the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, at that time a great number of bhikṣus were assembled and seated in the hall, engaging in this discussion:

"Venerable sirs, the Blessed One has previously, by means of countless approaches, taught the twelvefold dependent origination; therein, he first expounded ignorance as the essential nature of the condition."
For what reason, among all the conditions for afflictions and formative factors (*saṃskāra*), is ignorance alone designated as the essential nature of the condition?
What superior distinction is seen in this ignorance?
While these bhikṣus were seated together in the hall, their discussion was not yet concluded.

During the day, the Blessed One was dwelling in meditative practice; with his purified divine ear, which surpasses that of humans, he heard their discussion. In the afternoon, he arose from his meditation and went to that hall. Upon arrival, he stood before the assembly of bhikṣus and sat upon the seat usually prepared for him.
When they had finished sitting, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!
For what reason have you gathered here in the hall and remained seated with your discussion unfinished? What was the discussion you were having as you sat gathered here?"
The bhikṣus said:
"Venerable Sir!
A great number of bhikṣus have gathered and are sitting in the hall, engaging in this discussion, saying:"

"O living beings, the World-Honored One has previously, through countless approaches, taught the twelvefold dependent origination; therein, at the very beginning, he proclaimed ignorance as the causal essence."
By what cause and condition, among all the various formations conditioned by the afflictions, is ignorance alone designated as the essential nature of the condition?
What superior distinction is seen in this ignorance?
"Venerable Sir!
While we many bhikṣus were gathered and seated in the hall, our discussion was not yet concluded when such a discussion arose among us as we sat here together.
When he had spoken thus, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There is a dharma-gate called ‘The Initial Excellent Division of Dependent Origination. Listen well and reflect well, and I shall explain it to you.
What is this dharma-gate of the Initial Excellent Division of Dependent Origination?”
"O Bhikṣus!
Because it is the most preeminent among eleven kinds of preeminence, ignorance is established as the primary condition for dependent origination.
What are these eleven?"

That is to say: the excellence of the object of focus (*ālambana*), the excellence of the variety of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the excellence of the causal nexus (*nidāna*), the excellence of the origination (*samutthāna*), the excellence of the process of arising (*abhinirvṛtti*), the excellence of the inversion (*viparyāsa*), the excellence of the marks (*nimitta*), the excellence of the karma (*karman*), the excellence of the obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), the excellence of the conforming fetters (*anubandha*), and the excellence of the remedies (*pratipakṣa*).
At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, adjusted his robe over one shoulder, approached the Blessed One with palms joined and body bowed, and said:
"Venerable Sir!"
“What is the distinction regarding the objective condition of ignorance?
The Buddha said, “Monk!”
"Monks! All defiled portions, consisting of both causes and effects, as well as all purified portions, consisting of both causes and effects, are equally objects of appropriation for ignorance."
"This is the distinction regarding the objective condition (*ālambana*) of ignorance.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!"
“What is the distinction among the types of ignorance?
The Buddha said, “Monk!”
It conceals the real and manifests the unreal.
Monks! This is the specific distinction of the category of ignorance.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir,
what is the preeminent root of ignorance?"
The Buddha said:

“Monk! Because it serves as the preliminary cause, the root, and the dwelling place for all defilements of affliction (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), defilements of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), and defilements of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*).”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir,
what is the defilement of all afflictions?”
The Buddha said:

“Monks, briefly stated, there are three kinds of afflictions that defile all afflictions: namely, the affliction of lack of wisdom, the affliction of doubtful wisdom, and the affliction of false wisdom.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir,
what is meant by ‘all defilements of karma’?”
The Buddha said: “Bhikṣus!

Briefly stated, there are three distinctions of specific characteristics, namely: body, speech, and mind; as well as three distinctions of the characteristics of obstacles and their remedies. ‘Obstacles’ refers to non-merit; ‘remedies’ refers to merit and the imperturbable. These collectively encompass the defilement of karma.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir,
what is the defilement that arises in every way?”
The Buddha said: “Monks!

Briefly stated, the three feelings (namely, painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling) depend upon the three kinds of suffering (namely, the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the suffering of formations), which collectively encompass the defilement of birth.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
How is it that all these forms of defilement—defilement by afflictions, defilement by karma, and defilement by birth—all have ignorance as their thread, their root, and their abode?”
The Buddha said:
“Monks! Because of two kinds of delusion regarding the True Realities (satya), they cause afflictions that have not yet arisen to arise, and those already arisen to gradually increase and multiply.”
It causes unarisen karmic defilements to arise, and if they have already arisen, it further accumulates them;
it causes unarisen birth-defilements to arise, and if they have already arisen, they cannot be diverted.

Therefore it is said that all forms of defilement—defilement by afflictions, defilement by karma, and defilement by birth—all have ignorance as their preliminary cause, their root, and their abiding place.
“Monks! This is the preeminent source of ignorance.
The monks addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable One!
What is the distinction regarding the origination of ignorance?
The Buddha said:

“Monks! This ignorance is a condition that gives rise to delusion regarding the body yet to be born, which is subsumed under the truth of suffering in future lives; it is also a condition that gives rise to delusion regarding the body already obtained, which is subsumed under the truth of suffering in the present life. Because of this delusion, there is the gathering together of dependent origination and the proceeding forth of dependent origination; through their combination, there is gathering together and proceeding forth. Both of these two types of dependent origination—the delusion regarding the two bodies of the future and the present—have ignorance as their primary conditioning cause.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
What is the collection that gathers together the conditions of dependent origination?”
The Buddha said:

“Monks! First, ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; and likewise, name-and-form, the six sense bases, and contact condition feeling. This is called the gathering of conditions for the arising of the gathering of aggregates.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir,
what is this ‘proceeding by way of the conjunction of conditions’ that proceeds forth?”
The Buddha said: “Bhikṣus!

Within the second dependent origination based on ignorance, conditioned by feeling there is craving; conditioned by craving there is grasping; thus, conditioned by existence there is birth, and so on, up to: conditioned by birth there is old age and death. This is called the forward progression of the conjunction of dependent origination.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir,
how does initial ignorance act as the condition for arising within that collection of conditions and the collection of harmonious formations?”
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu!

This one, regarding the body subject to renewed existence, being deluded and lacking understanding, seeks renewed existence. Because he seeks renewed existence through such delusion, he perceives favorable things within that renewed existence."

However, regarding present objects of affection and aversion, due to attachment and conceptualization, one performs non-meritorious actions; that is to say, by giving rise to craving for various requisites and being associated with hatred toward harm and affliction, one fails to maintain deliberation regarding what is good or bad, and thus engages in heedless and deluded conduct.
Not perceiving through reflection the evil consequences in future lives, non-virtuous formations take ignorance as their condition.
Furthermore, if one perceives something favorable or perceives the path to liberation within the context of renewed existence, one then performs virtuous and immovable formations.

Whether through awakening through the teaching of the Dharma or through practicing meditative recollection for oneself, although there may be a wholesome mind within that awakening and recollection, it is not right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
Because of this, one is led away by the further arising of delusion.
That is to say, because one perceives favorable things within rebirth, one is not timid; because one perceives the path leading out [of suffering], one is not timid.

Those formations—meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable—which consist of adverse conditions and their antidotes, arise and perish together with the six groups of consciousness; thus, they are established within the arising and perishing of the resultant consciousness in the present.
Because all seeds newly produced after being perfumed are grasped through association, once all seeds have been grasped, their subsequent production follows a specific sequence;
that is, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and so forth, shall be produced gradually.

In this present retributive consciousness, those factors such as name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and so forth are merely the characteristics of the cause for arising and are not yet the characteristics of the fruit; therefore, it is called "appropriating dependent origination" (upādāna-pratītyasamutpāda).
"Monks! This is the first instance where ignorance acts as the condition for the arising of the aggregation of the conditions of dependent origination.
The monks addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable One!
How does subsequent ignorance act as the causal condition for the emergence of the conjunction of dependent origination?
The Buddha said:
“Monks! This is the delusion that arises regarding the present body: taking the six sense bases and contact as conditions, feeling is produced, and one then relishes its flavor.”
Because one has experienced their flavor, one will seek out similar sensations in the future.
When there is such seeking, grasping arises; when craving for pleasant sensation serves as a condition, sensual grasping (*kāmopādāna*) is produced.
Regarding the term "grasping through desire," this refers to the conceptualization of desire.
With that as the primary condition, the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) subsequently arise.

Furthermore, if one takes new sensations as a condition, there arises a craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*) accompanied by a mode of practice characterized by aversion and detachment. It is not logical for such [craving] to be associated with aversion and detachment; rather, it relies upon craving. When one seeks non-existence through improper means, there arise the false view of renunciation (*naiṣkramya-mithyādṛṣṭi*), the false view of certainty (*niyama-mithyādṛṣṭi*), and two types of false views based on those two. These constitute four kinds [of grasping], which cause this craving to take up its objects as conditions.

If, moreover, one takes that grasping as a basis and has not yet attained freedom from desire, then at the time of death, these four views and the afflictions of the desire realm arise with the thirst for desire as their condition to produce grasping. Furthermore, if one is free from desire for the desire realm but not yet free from form, then the thirst for the form realm and the thirst for the formless realm will arise and persist constantly.
When afflictions arise within the form realm or the formless realm, grasping (upādāna) then arises in those respective realms.

Those afflictions of the form and formless realms, as well as these various views, produce grasping either with craving for the form realm as the condition or with craving for the formless realm as the condition.

Thus, because craving conditions grasping (*upādāna*), the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*)—which has already been perfumed by the various formations (*saṃskāra*)—arises together with that grasping.

Once it is encompassed by that grasping, all those previously accumulated formations and all cravings that have not yet been extinguished will manifest in their respective places, so as to cause one's own self to proceed forth.
Because of these causes and conditions there is birth; therefore, those volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are called "existence" (*bhava*), due to the power of grasping (*upādāna*).

Since the formations constitute existence, once one has died here, that which was previously gathered together proceeds forth as a condition for what is to be born. For this reason, it is said that birth is conditioned by existence.

Within the process of emergence, at the time of birth, the characteristics of the body undergo transformation and differ from what they were before; furthermore, upon reaching that limit, there is death, decline, and the exhaustion of the life-span. Therefore, it is said that birth is the condition for old age and death.
“Monks! This is the second instance of ignorance, which acts as the causal condition for the arising of the manifestation of dependent origination in its process of manifestation.
The monks addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable One!

For what reason do you exclude thirst (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) from the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), yet do not state them to be conditions for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*)?
The Buddha said:
“Monks! Thirst and grasping are severed because they are limited by their own respective realms.
Just as with thirst and grasping for the desire realm, one should not create form-realm or formless-realm formations as conditions, for they are not their domain.”

Just as there is craving for the immovable formations (*āneñjya-saṃskāra*), so too is it with the craving for the form realm (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); the craving for the formless realm within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm; and likewise, the craving for the form realm within the desire realm.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir,
for what reason do craving and grasping not serve as conditions for meritorious and non-meritorious formations?”
The Buddha said:

“Monks! Regarding all present objects here before you, with the pleasant and the unpleasant as the predominant factors, through craving and thirst, one gives rise to unwholesome roots and performs non-meritorious actions.”

Because one does not recognize the evil within non-meritorious formations—which have both common and specific causes—namely, the evil of the mind and the evil of action, one gives rise to non-meritorious formations due to this lack of knowledge.
Furthermore, that mind and the evil deeds it commits have ignorance alone as their condition, not craving, because they do not share the same objective sphere as the unwholesome roots.

If one performs meritorious formations out of craving for sensual desire, it is done based on faith—namely, the faith that death is inevitably followed by rebirth and that rebirth necessarily depends upon conditions. Because these are governed by faith, the craving and grasping involved are merely designated by me as "obscured-unspecified" (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*); if a phenomenon is obscured-unspecified, it is incapable of initiating formative activity.

Because one does not know the renunciation within meritorious formations that share common causes and effects, one seeks a desirable rebirth and thus performs meritorious formations; therefore, although they are called "meritorious formations," they likewise have ignorance as their condition.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir,
for what reason does craving and grasping in the form realm not serve as a condition for the immovable karma of the form realm?"
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus! For one who has not yet abandoned desire, craving for form has not yet arisen, nor has it found a place to abide."

Because that [craving] does not yet exist, it has not yet attained its locus; therefore, it cannot serve as a condition for the imperturbable formations (*āniñjya-saṃskāra*) of the form realm to arise.

Just as craving for the form realm functions within the imperturbable formations of the form realm, so too does craving for the formless realm function within the imperturbable formations of the formless realm.

Because one perceives something favorable within the faults of the body of the form realm and the body of the formless realm, one conceives of them and reflects upon them; whether due to preaching the Dharma or instructing in the Dharma, such improper reflection arises and serves as a condition for that conduct.

However, this improper mental attention is induced by ignorance; as the fruit of improper mental attention, it combines with ignorance and serves as a condition for immovable formations (*āneñjya-saṃskāra*). Therefore, it should be understood that those immovable formations likewise have ignorance as their condition.

"Monks! Furthermore, because one relies on the absence of craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*), one performs meritorious deeds and deeds leading to the imperturbable (*āniñjya*). Due to this absence of craving for existence, one perceives the faults and evils of all states of existence; how then could one be willing to seek further rebirth?"

Furthermore, because they do not know non-existence as it truly is, and because they have not yet attained the path of antidotes due to this lack of true knowledge, they mistake what is not an antidote for the notion of an antidote, and consequently perform meritorious actions and immovable actions.
“Monks! By this causal sequence, you should know that it is only with ignorance as a condition that volitional formations arise, and not with craving or grasping as conditions.
The monks addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable One!
If [the formations] arise in conjunction with the six groups of consciousness, why do you say that formations have consciousness as their condition?
The Buddha said:

“Monks! Within these six groups of consciousness, meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formations arise and cease together in conjunction. They deposit the perfuming of formations within the resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), acting as the inducing means for the subsequent production of a new and distinct resultant consciousness. Therefore, it is said that ‘formations have consciousness as their condition.’”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!

Since the factors of name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling all simultaneously gather their seeds within consciousness, for what reason are they taught according to a sequential order?”
The Buddha said,
“Monks! Because they arise in succession in the future.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:

“Venerable Sir, for what reason are name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling called *jāti*? If the meaning is translated as ‘birth,’ does this refer to the general designation for the period before death within a single lifetime, rather than the initial moment of taking birth?”
The Buddha said:
"Monks! It is because they share the same basis for enjoyment and because they share the same cause for enjoyment."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!
If it were only name that gives rise to the formless, what fault would there be?"
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! If name does not abide within form, then the continuity of dhyāna and karma would be inconsistent."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
If it were only form that arises without a name, what fault would there be?”
The Buddha said:
“Monks! If form were not conjoined with name, and were not sustained by it, then it would perish and could not increase.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!
If consciousness alone were the condition for the six sense bases, what fault would there be?"
The Buddha said:

"Bhikṣu! At the very beginning, before the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) have been fulfilled, there exist only the body faculty (kāyendriya) and the mind faculty (manendriya); that which arises from their transformation cannot yet be found."

The substance of these two faculties consists solely of name-and-form at the initial stage; because they serve as the sequential conditions for the fulfillment of those six sense bases, it is said that "name-and-form is the condition for the six sense bases."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
If the mere fulfillment of the six sense bases constitutes the ultimate perfection of the dhyāna-yoga, for what reason do you further speak of contact and sensation?”
The Buddha said:

“Bhikṣu! Regarding this ‘ultimate refinement of the six sense bases’ (*ṣaḍāyatana-dhyāna-mardana*), it is the ultimate of the basis for experience (*upabhoga-niśraya*) while not yet being experienced; that which is necessarily the ultimate of experience itself is the reception through a common cause. Therefore, one should know that it is called the ‘ultimate refinement of dhyāna’ because it is both the ultimate of the basis for experience and the ultimate of experience.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!
This [teaching] states that craving is conditioned by ignorance, yet it also says that craving is conditioned by feeling."
“If it were only ignorance that conditions craving, rather than feeling being the condition,
what fault would there be? The Buddha said, “Monk!

The three types of thirst and the three types of existence arise simultaneously; however, because thirst is conditioned by feeling (*vedanā*), they do not arise if their mutual dependence lacks the necessary force. Therefore, it is not the case that thirst arises solely conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*).
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
If feeling alone were the condition for craving, what fault would there be?”
The Buddha said:

"Bhikṣus! All forms of thirst have feeling as their condition; yet there are also feelings that are not conditions for thirst, but rather serve as the condition for the cessation of all thirst. Therefore, it is not the case that thirst is conditioned by feeling alone."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
If existence were conditioned solely by craving and not by grasping, what fault would there be?”
The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus! Thirst is called 'seeking.

In those evil realms, there is certainly no seeking; yet one performs deeds that do not produce merit. Although one seeks a happy realm, it is always contrary to that [seeking]. When the fruit arises in rebirth, thirst is not the condition; rather, it is by taking up conditions of its own accord that it causes rebirth."
What the bhikṣu calls "being without thirst" is termed "being without seeking.
Although this absence of seeking appears contradictory [to the production of results], the fruit of meritorious and immovable actions nevertheless continues to arise.
"Monks! For this reason, it is not only craving that conditions existence.
The monks addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable One!
If grasping conditions becoming and becoming conditions birth, why do you not designate that grasping and becoming as the Truth of Origination?
The Buddha said:
“Monks! Because craving can perform four kinds of karma:
first, within the sensations of its own objective sphere, it performs the karma of binding through the attachment to deliciousness;”
Second, it performs the karma of equal engagement within grasping conditioned by craving;
third, it performs the karma of attraction within becoming conditioned by formations;
fourth, it performs the karma of continuous bondage after death.
"Therefore, it is said that craving alone is the truth of origination.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!"

There is birth, there is old age, and there is death; why then are the characteristics of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) all manifested under the designation of "old age and death"?
The Buddha said:
“Bhikṣu! That which constitutes the characteristic of arising is manifested as being bound in accordance with the three types of suffering.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir,
by what suffering is birth manifested?”
The Buddha said:
"Monks! This is a manifestation of the suffering inherent in conditioned existence."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir,
by what suffering is old age manifested?”
The Buddha said:
"Monk! This is a manifestation of the suffering inherent in change."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir,
by what suffering is death manifested?"
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! This is the manifestation of suffering upon suffering."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
Regarding all four modes of birth, what is the distinction between them and birth, old age, and death?”
The Buddha said:

“Monks! Those four modes of arising occur in successive order; as they arise, they arise in accordance with their respective similarities. You should understand that such is the nature of the characteristic of arising within the process of arising.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
The signs of birth arise in succession; to what are they comparable?”
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus! When that seed is first sown, it immediately undergoes birth; it then grows and develops through successive stages."
That which emerges from the womb arises in succession; that which has emerged grows in succession.
Having grown, it is able to experience worldly existence.
From whom, then, does this successive arising arise?
The aggregates, elements, and sense bases arise without a self. Why is this?
Because the five aggregates and so forth increase, shift, and flow, being impermanent;
furthermore, the life-faculty, power, measure, time, and duration are likewise produced by impermanence.
“Monks! When those four signs of birth are broken down by time, they become fivefold decay; this is called ‘old age.
The monks addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable One!
What are the five kinds of decline and corruption?
The Buddha said:
“Monks! First, the hair becomes decrepit and spoiled because it has lost its color and deteriorated;
second, the physical basis becomes decrepit and spoiled—the ‘basis’ refers to the body—because the flesh, complexion, and vitality have declined.”

Third, the decline of karma: because one gasps for breath when speaking; because one’s back bends like that of a humpbacked ox when standing; because one’s body leans forward heavily when sitting; because one must lean on a staff when walking; and because mental intelligence is bound and mindfulness is weak and diminished.

Fourth, the decline of enjoyment: because one enjoys inferior things among present requisites; because one does not enjoy any of the pleasures that are usually delightful; and because the sensory faculties do not function swiftly or even fail to function within their own respective domains.
Fifth, the decline of the life-faculty: because the lifespan is exhausted and death is near; and because one cannot endure even minor causes of death.
"Monks! Within those four modes of birth, you should know that there are also six distinctions of death: first, death at the completion of the lifespan;

second, death before the completion of the lifespan; third, death by its own characteristic; fourth, the portion of death before the completion of the lifespan; fifth, the portion of death at the completion of the lifespan; and sixth, untimely death."

"Monks! Among these, one who dies by way of natural characteristics should be understood as follows: consciousness departs from the body to another state, and the material sense-faculties perish and vanish."
“Bhikṣu! There is this distinction between the characteristics of the arising of name-and-form and so forth, and [the characteristics of] birth, old age, and death.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
You have stated that all three types of craving are conditioned arising and serve as causes for birth; why then do you speak only of birth in the desire realm?
The Buddha said:
“Monks! Because birth in the desire realm is coarse, it is not to be praised nor can it be taught as knowledge; for it is a state of returning, not the essence of the dharma of liberation.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!

If these twelve links are explained as the gathering of conditions for dependent origination and their subsequent manifestation, among them, how many are the links that perform the gathering, and how many are the links that are gathered?"
“How many are the factors that cause emergence, and how many are the factors that constitute what emerges?
The Buddha said, “Bhikṣus!”
Ignorance, volitional formations, and a portion of consciousness constitute the "appropriating aggregate";
that same portion of consciousness, along with name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling, constitute the "appropriated aggregate."
"Monks! That one portion consisting of feeling, craving, clinging, and becoming is the factor that turns out;

birth and aging-and-death are the factors turned out by it. Furthermore, that one portion consisting of name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling should also be known as factors turned out by it."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
These factors of gathering together and these factors of emerging forth—can they be seen as arising simultaneously, or must they occur sequentially?”
The Buddha said:
"Monks! They arise simultaneously; they are explained in succession."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!

Since the factors of gathering together and the factors of turning out arise simultaneously, why is it that the factors of gathering together are mentioned first, and the factors of turning out are mentioned later?”
The Buddha said:
“Monks! Because there is further emergence from what is gathered by grasping, therefore there is nothing that does not arise from what is gathered by grasping.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
Since ignorance conditions improper reflection, for what reason do you say that it acts as a condition for ignorance?”
The Buddha said, “Monks!

Because ignorance, having been drawn forth by improper attention, acts as a condition for volitional formations; from ignorance arise contact and feeling, which in turn act as conditions for craving.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir,
by how many characteristics can dependent origination be known in brief?”
The Buddha said:
“Monks, the dependent origination characterized by three marks can be understood in brief:”

First is the characteristic of immovable dependent origination; *nirīha* is translated as "immovable," and it signifies emptiness, for because it is empty, there is no movement or action. Second is the characteristic of impermanent dependent origination. Third is the characteristic of capable dependent origination.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!

There are four kinds of conditions as taught by the Blessed One: namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*, formerly called the sequential condition), the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*, also called the productive condition).”
"Venerable Sir!
Among these, by what condition does ignorance serve as a condition for volitional formations?
And so on, up to: by what condition does birth serve as a condition for aging and death?"
The Buddha said:
"Monks! Because all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) arise through a common characteristic of transformation, I have taught the four kinds of conditions."
In this context, it is solely as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) that I intend to say "ignorance conditions volitional formations" up to "birth conditions aging and death.
Furthermore, that dominant condition is of two kinds: non-attachment and attachment.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!
What is this predominant condition of non-attachment?"
"What is the predominant condition for attachment to signs?
The Buddha said, "Monks!"
"Monks! When improper attention has not yet arisen, the latent tendency of ignorance serves as a condition for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) without being attached to them;
once it has arisen, it becomes attached."

When that improper attention conjoins with formations, it arises together with the six groups of consciousness; while it has arisen but not yet ceased, it acts as a condition for consciousness without being attached to it;
once it has arisen and ceased, they become mutually attached.

"Monks! All consciousness that has not yet reached the time of death does not become attached to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as its condition; rather, it becomes a condition for name-and-form through attachment. [This phrase is also absent in the Sanskrit original. Just as consciousness relates to name-and-form, so too is the gathering together of name-and-form, and likewise the manifestation of name-and-form."
As it is with name-and-form in relation to name-and-form, so it is with the six sense bases in relation to the six sense bases, contact in relation to contact, and feeling in relation to feeling.
As it is with ignorance in relation to volitional formations, so it is with ignorance in relation to craving, craving in relation to clinging, and clinging in relation to existence.
Just as consciousness relates to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), so it is with name-and-form relating to name-and-form and the like; likewise, existence (*bhava*) relates to birth (*jāti*).
Furthermore, monks!
Within birth, the stages of the embryo, childhood, and youth do not adhere to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), yet they act as its conditions.
"If one reaches the time when the faculties have matured and the lifespan is exhausted, it should be understood that they act as conditions for one another.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!"
If the Blessed One, within the Dharma-gate of common causes, common conditions, and common bases, taught karma on account of craving, what was the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) therein?
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus! As for the statement that 'karma is subsumed under existence,' this is spoken because of craving; this is the underlying intention."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
By what principle may this be seen?”
"By what meaning can it be seen?
By what meaning can it be seen?
The Buddha said:
“Monks! Because it establishes the seeds for future rebirths, the meaning of ‘cause’ (hetu) can be seen;
because it definitively sustains that birth so that it emerges, the meaning of ‘condition’ (pratyaya) can be seen.”
"Because one has already died and then emerges toward a place of birth for the sake of being born, this can be seen through the meaning.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!"
“Monk, what is the meaning of the phrase ‘arising through conditions’?
The Buddha said: “Monk!”
Because each has its own conditions, they gather together and continue in succession; thus, these various factors arise.
*The Sūtra on the Primary Factors of Dependent Origination*, Volume Upper.
*The Sūtra on the Primary Factors of Dependent Origination*, Volume Lower.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
A bhikṣu addressed the Buddha: “Venerable Sir! Is it only this arising in succession that constitutes dependent origination, or is there yet another dependent origination?”
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus! I teach dependent origination through eight gateways:"

First is that which refers to the experience of conventional reality (*saṃvṭti*), such as when the eye conditions visible forms to produce visual consciousness; from the conjunction of these three arises contact (*sparśa*), and conditioned by contact arises sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth.

Second is that which refers to dependent origination as the support of sustenance, such as when the four nutriments (*āhāra*) act as conditions, enabling the sense faculties and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) to persist and undergo increase.

Third is that which refers to dependent origination as the cause of support, such as when seeds within various grains, through the conditions of the field and water, give rise to sprouts and the like.

The fourth refers to the dependent origination of that which is produced and connected; it is like the stage of gathering and the stage of emerging, as they pertain to what is gathered and what emerges during production.

The fifth refers to the dependent origination of that which is produced and connected within the state of production; it is like the world, which can be understood to undergo formation and destruction through causes and conditions.

The sixth refers to the dependent origination of those who enter into production; it is like the distinction between the three evil destinies and the destinies of gods and humans, which can be understood to arise due to unwholesome and wholesome contaminated karma.

The seventh refers to explaining dependent origination for those who seek purification: by taking the voices of others and one’s own correct reflection as causes, right view arises; because of this, ignorance ceases. Because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease, and so on, until birth ceases, whereby aging and death cease.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
Just as ignorance conditions volitional formations and so forth arise in succession, does their cessation likewise occur in succession in this same way?”
The Buddha said,
“Monk, it is not so.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir,
for what reason did he teach cessation in this sequential order?"
The Buddha said:
"Monks! Because the preceding portion possesses the capacity for non-arising, the subsequent portion manifests as the dharma of non-arising."
"Monks! There is no phenomenon that does not arise which then undergoes cessation and transformation.

Eighth, it is said that the one who possesses mastery speaks of dependent origination: just as a monk who has well-cultivated reflection, cultivated concentration, and cultivated practice as conditions—if he so desires, according to his faith and understanding, then it is exactly thus and not otherwise."
“Monks! This is what I call the eightfold gateway of dependent origination.
The monks addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!
If the Blessed One has said that birth occurs because of karma and that one proceeds [into existence] because of craving, with what underlying intention did he speak thus?"
The Buddha said: "Monk!

Due to the condition of ignorance, various meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formations (*saṃskāra*) were previously performed and accumulated within existence. These gather and encompass the seeds for the arising of various bodily experiences. Within this, craving has not yet been eliminated; because of that craving, that body emerges again within existence. Those formations have the power [to produce birth] and are not without craving; therefore, it is said that birth is received due to karma, and emergence occurs due to craving."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!
If it is due to craving that [existence] proceeds forth, why is it that existence has grasping as its condition, rather than craving?"
The Buddha said:

“Monks! If there were craving but no grasping, it could not serve as a condition for birth in the woeful realms through unwholesome formations. Furthermore, if there were no craving and no grasping, it could not serve as a condition for birth in the two kinds of happy realms—whether in the non-concentrated states or the concentrated states—through wholesome or imperturbable formations. Therefore, it is not only craving that conditions becoming; grasping also conditions becoming.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
If the World-Honored One has previously spoken within the Great Exposition of the Dharma Gate, saying:”

"Ānanda! Among those various classes of sentient beings therein, some are not born while others are born; it can likewise be known that if all such classes lack the conditions for birth, then aging and death will also be absent."
“World-Honored One!
With what underlying intention did you speak thus?
The Buddha said:

“Monks! This was spoken with intentional meaning: that birth as a collection and birth as an emergence are the predominant conditions for aging and death; non-attachment and attachment—this is the intentional meaning.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
The Blessed One has already explained the phrasing of dependent origination, but has not yet explained the meaning of dependent origination. How is that to be understood?”
The Buddha said: “Monks!

Briefly stated, there are eleven aspects of the meaning of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) that can be seen: namely, the meaning of being without an agent, the meaning of having common causes, the meaning of being without a sentient being, the meaning of arising from another, the meaning of immobility, the meaning of impermanence, the meaning of momentary emptiness, the meaning of the uninterrupted succession of cause and effect, the meaning of diverse causes and effects, the meaning of similar causes and effects, and the meaning of determinate causes and effects.”
"This is the meaning of dependent origination; it should be viewed in this way.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!"
“If the Blessed One has indeed spoken of that which is profound, it is this very dependent origination. But how, Bhikṣu, can this profound dependent origination be seen?
The Buddha said: “Bhikṣu!”

Thus, by means of these eleven types of meaning, five kinds of profundity are to be seen: namely, profundity of cause, profundity of characteristic, profundity of arising, profundity of abiding and transformation, and profundity of manifestation and progression.

"Monks! Furthermore, there are five kinds of profound dependent origination that can be seen: namely, profundity of characteristics, profundity of the inclusion of seeds, profundity of causes, profundity of results, and profundity of the distinctions in the application of causes and results as antidotes."

"Monks! Furthermore, there are five kinds of profound dependent origination that can be seen: namely, profundity of synthesis, profundity of direct order, profundity of reverse order, profundity of grasping, and profundity of the objective sphere."
“Monks! This is the excellence of the origination of ignorance.
The monks addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable One!
What is the excellence of the transformation and abiding of ignorance?
The Buddha said:

“Bhikṣus! Briefly stated, there are four modes of manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā*): namely, the mode of latent tendency (formerly called *anuśaya*), the mode of active arising (formerly called *bandhana*, also termed *paryavasthāna*), the mode of association, and the mode of independent, non-associated occurrence.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir,
by whom is ignorance turned and established so as to act as a condition?"
The Buddha said:
"Monks! Furthermore, an ordinary person, through improper reflection, draws forth four kinds of ignorance, which act as conditions for meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formations."
"Monks! Furthermore, even if an ordinary person possesses a mind of wholesome karma associated with merit or the imperturbable, it is still the flow of unrighteous reflection. Monks!"

Regarding this internal dharma, for the heedless worldling—setting aside the unique ignorance (āveṇikī avidyā) for a moment—it is that other ignorance and heedlessness which act as the conditions that draw forth the formative forces (saṃskāra).
O Bhikṣu!

In this internal dharma, when ordinary persons in training and noble ones in training are heedless, their false thoughts induce three kinds of ignorance which serve as conditions for non-merit; however, that non-merit cannot produce existence in the miserable realms. Therefore, that non-merit is not "formations conditioned by ignorance."

I have previously stated that there is a unique ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) which ordinary persons who practice heedfulness within this internal Dharma have not yet abandoned, whereas noble learners (*śaikṣa*) have already abandoned it.

When such an ordinary person who practices heedfulness generates meritorious or immovable formations (*puṇya-āneñjya-saṃskāra*), and gives rise to a mind associated with right reflection (*samyak-cintā*) regarding the True Dharma, at that time they also generate the causes for liberation and the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*). Due to the predominance of these, they will emerge from birth in the two happy destinies (*sugati*); however, because they have not yet abandoned the predominance of the four types of ignorance, [they remain bound].

"Monks! However, because the noble disciple has abandoned the unique ignorance (āveṇikā-avidyā) and does not create new karma, even if all past karma remains due to the power of latent tendencies (anuśaya), he will reach its final exhaustion through repeated contact. Thus, for him, the production of formations conditioned by ignorance gradually diminishes and no longer increases."
For this reason, it should be understood that those who train in this inner Dharma do not produce volitional formations conditioned by ignorance. Bhikṣus!

It is for the sake of these external worldlings that I speak of the arising of defiled dependent origination in its progressive fulfillment; it is not for the sake of those who train in this inner Dharma.
“Monks! This is the excellence of the persistence of ignorance.
The monks addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable One!
What is the excellence of the inversion of ignorance?
The Buddha said:
“Monks! These four kinds of ignorance consist of two types of perversions: superimposing existence upon what does not exist within the Truths, and denying existence to what does exist.
The monks addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable One!
What are these two kinds of perversions: imputing existence to what does not exist, and deprecating existence by claiming it does not exist?
The Buddha said:

“Monks! Due to four kinds of causes and conditions—namely, seeing what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, seeing the Dharma as not the Dharma, regarding the heavenly realms and liberation as non-expedient means when they are expedient means—there is the perversion of superimposing existence upon what does not exist.
Because of wrong view, one universally slanders by saying ‘it does not exist’; this is the perversion of denying existence where it exists.”
“Monks! This is the excellence of the perversion of ignorance.
The monks addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable One!
What is the excellence of the characteristics of ignorance?
The Buddha said:

“Monks! There are two kinds of visible objects: first, the distinction of subtle self-characteristics; second, the distinction of common characteristics regarding the objects of the inverted views of the pleasant, the unpleasant, and that which is both.”

"Monks! Thus, all instances of the arising of ignorance are subtle, difficult to know, and difficult to see; how much more so for that which conforms to latent tendencies? Furthermore, all associated ignorance is subtle, difficult to know, and difficult to see; how much more so for that which is non-associated? Within the spheres of the attractive, the unattractive, and both—which are objects of inversion—it conceals the true nature and manifests as inverted perceptions, functioning with equal force."
The remaining afflictions are not like this; even other afflictions of a similar nature, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), arise only by taking that ignorance as their basis.
“Bhikṣus!
This is the preeminent characteristic of ignorance.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable One!
What is the excellence of the activity of ignorance?
The Buddha said:
“Monks! In brief, you should know that ignorance has two kinds of functions:
first, ignorance is that which acts as the basis for the arising and turning of all seeds.”
"Second, ignorance is that which turns all seeds away and acts as an obstacle.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha,
"Venerable Sir!"
“What is it that causes all these various types to arise and evolve?
The Buddha said, “Monk!”
"If there is arising in a place, or arising as it arises, this is called the activation of all seeds.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!"
"In what place will he be reborn?
The Buddha said, "O Bhikṣu!"
"It is because of the conceptualization of a self within the path of saṃsāra.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!"
"By what dharma is there further arising?
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu!"
“Because the internal and external sense bases are grasped by means of a self.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!”
"How does rebirth occur?
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu!"
“Karma and its retribution continue to arise and evolve because of self-conceptualization and false conceptualization.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha,
“Venerable Sir!”
"What is the turning away from all seeds?
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu!"
Briefly stated, there are four kinds of turning away:
namely, first, turning away from the basis; second, turning away from the object of focus; third, turning away from mental attention; and fourth, turning away from the accomplishment of the fruit.
“Monks! This is the excellence of the activity of ignorance.
The monks addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable One!
What is the excellence of the adversary to ignorance?
The Buddha said:
“Monks! The noble Dharma is the adversary of ignorance, and the extensive Dharma is the adversary of ignorance; these two should be seen as such.
The monks addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable One!
What is the adverse condition for the supreme Dharma that is ignorance?
The Buddha said:

“Monks! Among these five faculties, it is by means of this and through this that they are grasped and unified—namely, the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya). Its direct opposite is ignorance (avijjā); therefore, it is called the ‘adverse factor to the superior dhamma.’”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir,
how is it that ignorance is the adverse condition for the vast Dharma?"
The Buddha said:

“Monks! Whatever constitutes the wisdom of the essence of hearing, the wisdom of the essence of reflection, and the wisdom of the essence of cultivation—their adverse counterpart is ignorance; therefore, it is called the ‘adverse counterpart to the vast Dharma.’”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
If it is said that the absence of wisdom is ignorance, would there not then be a case where such ignorance does not exist?”
The Buddha said,
“Monk, it is not so.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!
If wisdom were not this ignorance, what fault would there be?"
The Buddha said:
"Monk! If that were so, the characteristic of ignorance could not be established."
Why is this? Bhikṣus!

The wisdom of the essence of hearing lacks the wisdom of the essence of reflection; the wisdom of the essence of reflection lacks the wisdom of the essence of cultivation. The mundane wisdom of the essence of cultivation lacks the supramundane wisdom of the essence of cultivation; the supramundane wisdom of training lacks the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣa). The wisdom of a śrāvaka beyond training lacks the wisdom of a Tathāgata.
One who is thus is both possessed of wisdom and devoid of wisdom; it is because of such ignorance that their characteristics can be established.
Furthermore, O Bhikṣu!

Among the three roots of goodness, I speak of non-delusion (*amoha*). Within that state, delusion is absent and thus there is non-delusion; it is not that the absence of delusion itself constitutes non-delusion.

Likewise, it is not that the absence of clarity constitutes ignorance (*avidyā*); rather, because the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) do not know reality, they are called ignorance, just as because the mental factors do know reality, they are called wisdom (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, monks!
If this ignorance did not exist, then these eleven specific types of superior ignorance would not exist either. Therefore, that which is the absence of knowledge is what constitutes ignorance.
“Monks! This is the excellence of the opposition to ignorance.
The monks addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable One!
What is the excellence of the fetters concordant with ignorance?
The Buddha said:

“Bhikṣus! As far as the beings of the three realms, up to those in the Peak of Existence, if they have not yet attained wisdom regarding these Truths, they are bound by latent tendencies that are unbroken and pervasive; for that reason, those beings are said to be ‘bound in their entirety.’”

Furthermore, within the causal divisions of the happy and miserable realms, there is likewise no wisdom; among them, those that are subtle belong to the formless realm, those that are intermediate to the form realm, and those that are superior to the desire realm. Yet these subtle, intermediate, and superior states are, by their very nature, bound to future existence.
Furthermore, monks!
If an Arhat has exhausted all outflows, that which constitutes an obstacle for him is likewise a fetter concordant with ignorance (*avidyā*).
This ignorance, which travels far and acts as a fetter, should also be seen in this way.
“Bhikṣus! This is the excellence of the fetter that accords with ignorance.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable One!
What is the excellence of the antidote to ignorance?
The Buddha said:

“Monks! There are two kinds of knowledge that serve as the antidote to ignorance: first, that which arises either through the voice of another or without it, which is the knowledge of the limited dharma-realm;
second, that which arises through the voice of another and is not limited, which is the knowledge of the immeasurable dharma-realm.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!
With respect to that limited wisdom regarding the dharma-dhātu, what is its object of focus?"
What are its characteristics?
What is its function?
How is it to be perceived?
The Buddha said:

“Bhikṣus! That limited wisdom of the dharma-realm takes the four foundations of mindfulness as its object and possesses sixteen aspects; though it is accompanied by ignorance, it performs the function of distancing one from the defilements of afflictions, karma, and birth. It should be viewed in this way.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir,
how is the suffering of birth to be perceived?"
The Buddha said:
“Monks! It is because of dependence on internal causes of suffering, dependence on external causes of suffering, and dependence on both those types of suffering.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!
What is internal causal suffering?"
The Buddha said:
"Monks, there is the suffering of illness, the suffering of old age, and the suffering of death."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir,
what is external causal suffering?”
The Buddha said:
"Monks! The suffering of being joined with what is not loved, the suffering of separation from what is loved, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir, what are those two bases of suffering?"
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! To speak briefly, there are the five aggregates of clinging."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir,
what is this craving (tṛṣṇā)?"
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! If there is craving within the present body."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir,
what is this craving for renewed existence?”
The Buddha said:
"Monks! If one has wishes and aspirations regarding a future body."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
What is this craving that accompanies the desire for delight?”
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! If one becomes attached to the flavors found within the present objects of experience that have been acquired and appropriated by oneself."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir,
what is this craving for sensual desire that delights in various objects?"
The Buddha said:
“Monks! If one pursues various things within the realm of what has not yet been attained.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!
Regarding this craving (tṛṣṇā), what is its complete abandonment without remainder?"
The Buddha said:

“Monks! That which should be abandoned through the vision of the Path is abandoned because of the abandonment of the afflictions; because of the abandonment of the lower and upper fetters; because of the abandonment of craving for future bitter fruits; and because of the abandonment of craving for present bitter fruits.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir, what is equanimity?"
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! That which is to be abandoned by seeing the Path is abandoned because the afflictions are abandoned."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir, what is this ultimate limit?”
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! If one cultivates the path that ought to be abandoned, it is abandoned because the afflictions are abandoned."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir, what is that which is exhausted?"
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! It is because the lower fetters have been severed that they are abandoned."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir, what is detachment?”
The Buddha said:
“Monk! They are abandoned because the higher fetters (ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana) are abandoned.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir! What is cessation?"
The Buddha said:
"Monks! If it is through ultimate severance that it is severed."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir,
what is this ‘quiescence’?”
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! As for future suffering and its fruits, they are abandoned because craving is abandoned."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir! What is this ‘disappearance’?”
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus! As for present suffering as a fruit, it is abandoned because craving is abandoned."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir, what is right view?”
The Buddha said:

“Bhikṣu! It is because one transcends the skillful means of the teachings and practices through the wisdom that precedes realization, the wisdom at the time of realization, and the subsequently attained wisdom.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir, what is right discernment?”
The Buddha said:

“Monks! Having attained right knowledge regarding the Three Jewels, and by virtue of relying on right faith, one reflects upon and discerns their qualities, thereby transcending various doctrines and teachings.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir, what is right speech?"
The Buddha said:

"Bhikṣu! If it is the morality cherished by the noble ones, which is comprised within the outflow-free (anāsrava) and functions in conjunction with outflow-free contemplation, one remains far removed from the four types of vocal karma because of transcending the evil destinies."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir, what is right action?”
The Buddha said:

“Bhikṣu! If it is the morality beloved by the noble ones, which is comprised within the outflow-free (anāsrava) and functions in conjunction with outflow-free reflection, it distances one from the three types of bodily action and transcends the evil destinies.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir, what is right livelihood?”
The Buddha said:

“Monks! If it is the morality beloved by the noble ones, which is comprised within the outflow-free (anāsrava) and proceeds together with outflow-free contemplation, it distances one from the bodily and vocal actions arising from wrong livelihood and transcends the evil destinies.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir,
what is right exertion?"
The Buddha said:
"Monks! If, within the higher liberations, one relies upon aspiration and desire, arouses diligence, distances oneself from adverse factors, and fulfills the remedies."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir, what is right mindfulness?"
The Buddha said:

"Bhikṣu! When one is in union with śamatha and vipaśyanā, having made these three types of signs the basis, one should from time to time enter into right abiding together with heedfulness within these three types of signs. One should not forget the mental factors regarding the objective condition, for in the cultivation of the path, one must transcend what is non-concordant."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir, what is right concentration?”
The Buddha said:

“Monks! If one thoroughly cultivates these seven kinds of concentration and directs the mind single-mindedly toward them, they serve as the basis for the practice of their various distinctions, and they serve as the basis for the arising of sublime qualities.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!

If that is so, since the foundations of mindfulness and all other factors of enlightenment are all subsumed within the Path, for what reason do you speak only of the Noble Eightfold Path as the characteristic of the Path?”
The Buddha said:
“Monks! Because of the Noble Eightfold Path, all other factors conducive to awakening (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are subsumed within it.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
If there are four characteristics within this suffering, which among them is the characteristic of impermanence?”
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! If one perceives within suffering the phenomena of arising and ceasing, this is its characteristic."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
What is the characteristic of suffering?”
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! Having taken that very nature of arising and ceasing as one's basis, if one perceives the three kinds of suffering as binding, this is its characteristic."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir,
what is the characteristic of emptiness?"
The Buddha said:
“Monk! If, within suffering, one perceives it as being devoid of a self or anything belonging to a self, this is its characteristic.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir,
what is the characteristic of non-self?”
The Buddha said:
“Monk! If, within suffering, one perceives the characteristic of self as being detached from it, this is its characteristic.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!
If these four types constitute the characteristic of origination (samudaya-lakṣaṇa), among them, which is the characteristic of cause (hetu-lakṣaṇa)?"
The Buddha said:
“Monk! If one perceives within craving the causal essence that sows the seeds of suffering, this is its characteristic.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir,
what is the characteristic of origination?”
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus! If one perceives within craving the essence that serves as the cause for the continuity of rebirth, this is its characteristic."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir,
what is the characteristic of arising?”
The Buddha said:
“Monk! If one perceives within craving the essential nature that serves as the cause for the differentiated arising of the five destinies, this is its characteristic.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
What is the characteristic of conditions?”
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! If, within craving, one perceives another distinct causal substance that maintains it, this is its characteristic."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
If this truth of cessation has four characteristics, among them, which one is the characteristic of cessation?”
The Buddha said:
“Monk! If one perceives the cessation of afflictions within liberation, this is its characteristic.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir,
what is the characteristic of stilling?”
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! If, within liberation, one perceives the cessation of suffering, this is its characteristic."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
What are these excellent marks?”
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! If one perceives within liberation that which is blameless, pure, and pleasant, this is its characteristic."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir,
what is the mark of emergence?"
The Buddha said:
“Monk! If one perceives impermanence as emerging within liberation, this is its characteristic.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!
If these four kinds constitute the characteristics of the Path, among them, which one is the characteristic of the Path?"
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus! Within this path, if one perceives what is known in accordance with reality and without inversion—this is its characteristic."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
What is the characteristic of suchness?”
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus! If, within this path, one perceives that which is supramundane and untainted, this is its characteristic."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
What is the characteristic of the track?”
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! If one perceives within the Noble Path that one is practicing in accordance with it, this is its characteristic."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
What is the characteristic of the vehicle?”
The Buddha said:
“Bhikṣu! If one perceives the unsurpassed within this path, this is its characteristic.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir,
for what reason are there only the Four Noble Truths?"
The Buddha said: “Monks!

Because both defilement and purification, together with their causes and effects, are all subsumed herein, they are called ‘shared. Regarding those that are shared: if there is defilement, then cause and effect are both defiled; if there is purification, then cause and effect are both purified. Therefore, they are called ‘shared.’”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!
Regarding these Truths, such as the Truth of Suffering and the others, for what reason are they taught in gradual succession?"
The Buddha said:
"Monks! Illness is like suffering; its cause is like the origin; freedom from it is like cessation; and the medicine is like the path."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir,
are these four noble truths realized and seen simultaneously, or are they realized and seen gradually?"
The Buddha said:

"Monks! Because there is a principle, one realizes and sees [the truth] all at once; because there is a principle, one realizes and sees it gradually. This principle is also called 'causal condition' (hetu-pratyaya) and is also called 'expedient means' (upāya)."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!
If they are realized and seen simultaneously, what is the underlying principle?"
The Buddha said:

"Bhikṣu! Within oneself, one knows the realm of the true wisdom of the truths; by taking as an object the non-established meaning through a collective apprehension, one realizes and perceives it all at once."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir,
if it is realized and seen through gradual stages, what is the underlying principle?"
The Buddha said:

“Bhikṣus! Having cultivated and refined both fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), one observes their characteristics through their specific marks (*svalakṣaṇa*) and causes and effects; because this is not a generalized object of focus, they are realized and seen progressively.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir,
if the World-Honored One has taught the Four Noble Truths, for what reason do you further speak of two truths?”
"What are the conventional truth and the ultimate truth?
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu!"
Among these Four Noble Truths, whatever phenomena constitute the domain of conventional knowledge (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*) belong to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);

whereas that which constitutes the domain of one's own internal knowledge of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-jñāna*), the domain of non-conceptualizing knowledge (*apratiṣṭhita-jñāna*), belongs to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
"One should see it in this way.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!"
If the Four Noble Truths are truths for both the non-noble and the noble, why are they called "noble truths," and why did the Blessed One speak of them as such?
The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus!
Although they are not noble ones, because they lack wisdom yet have faith within this very essence of the Truths;”
Because the Noble Ones possess wisdom and faith regarding this essential nature of phenomena,
for this reason it is called a "Noble Truth" and should be viewed in this way.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
Regarding the wisdom of the immeasurable dharma-realm that is not of a limited portion, what is its object of focus?”
"What are its characteristics?
What is its function?
The Buddha said:

“Monks! Furthermore, one takes the Four Noble Truths as the object of focus; taking the purification of perception regarding the Truths as its characteristic, taking the entry into the Truths in all their aspects as its characteristic, and taking the accomplishment of every benefit and welfare for all sentient beings as its characteristic.”

Furthermore, regarding those with limited knowledge of the dharma-realm: the śrāvaka is characterized by not having the welfare and benefit of sentient beings manifest before them, while the pratyekabuddha is characterized by turning their back on the welfare and benefit of sentient beings.
Furthermore, the wisdom of the immeasurable dharma-realm has "distancing" as its function, meaning it distances one from all types of afflictions and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*);
it has "providing a basis" as its function, meaning it serves as the basis for attaining the thoroughly purified dharma-realm of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*);
and it has "sheltering" as its function, meaning it shelters all sentient beings from the oppressions and afflictions of various states.
"Monks! This is the excellence of the antidote to ignorance. The monks said:
“Excellent, O Great Virtuous One!
Those bhikṣus, having heard what was spoken by the Blessed One, remained silent with joy.
Those bhikṣus, their hearts delighted by what the Blessed One had said, were all greatly filled with gladness.

yet, through accumulation, they become the three realms. The stream of delusion flows far and wide, and the tree of suffering grows tall and dense.

Exhausting the realm of provisional names, the five causes, seven fruits, and twelve links—the dharma of dependent origination—is fully contained herein.
The ordinary person is deluded and gives rise to falsehood; the sage awakens and penetrates the truth. The inferior is like a rabbit swimming;
the superior is like an elephant crossing [a river]. How great! The wondrous enlightenment is profound, thoroughly penetrating the ten stages and the two vehicles.
The forests, groves, cities, and rice fields are all fully spread; yet as for this sutra, it uniquely encompasses those examples.

What was not explained therein is here fully expounded. Taking "object-condition" (*ālambana*) as the beginning and "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*) as the end, there are eleven general sections in total and one hundred and twenty specific questions; its purport is subtle and profound.
Its phrasing is concise yet profound; the essential framework of the sutra is contained herein.

Furthermore, the sage Ullangha, following the intent of this sutra, composed a treatise to elucidate its meaning. This treatise universally draws upon the principles of the Three Vehicles without adhering to the literal traps of any single school.
First, it establishes verses in chapter form, and subsequently provides an expository commentary. The verses:
Because it consists of thirty [chapters], it is also called the *Triṃśatikā-śāstra*. In the tenth month of the second year of the Daye era,
the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta, together with the late Dharma Master Yancong, translated it at the Shanglin Garden in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang),
based on a Sanskrit manuscript of the *Triṃśatikā* obtained in the kingdom of Lin-yi— the former name for the country of Jambudvīpa (India) being erroneously transcribed as "Tianzhu."
Translated into the language of the Sui dynasty, the work was completed in the ninth month of the third year; it consists of two fascicles of sutra and one fascicle of treatise.

The Tripiṭaka Master—whose name is Lun Xianming—and Fayi of Shenmi, who were both profoundly learned in the scriptures and treatises and proficient in Sanskrit, compared the text against the palm-leaf manuscript, cross-examining and verifying each other until not a single word was omitted.
Having reviewed it three times with increasing care, the language is somewhat plain and simple, yet the intent remains faithful and correct.

Compared to the ancients, it is largely free from fault or error; truly, it may be called a lamp of the Dharma and sufficiently named a treasury of wisdom. May it benefit the world constantly until the end of time. Thus it is said.
